title: Funding Waterfall at the Vet Estimate
angle: Finance (payments, credit, insurance) x Pets & animal health (vet access, insurance)
one_liner: Front-desk software that routes each vet estimate to the cheapest available funding: insurance advance, charity grant, clinic plan, or credit.
customer: Independent and affordable-care vet clinics as the subscriber. Charitable funds and lenders are paying counterparties.
problem: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay. Funding sources exist but are fragmented: reimbursement-model insurers pay weeks later, dozens of small charity funds are unknown at the front desk, and mainstream medical credit charges clinics steep fees. New philanthropy has no distribution pipe, so grants like Duffield's are hard to place and audit.
solution: An 'estimate inbox' where the front desk emails or prints the estimate, with no PIMS integration. Within minutes it returns a ranked stack: (1) a 0% claim advance for insured pets secured by the expected reimbursement; (2) pre-screened charity or grant matches; (3) a clinic-carried 0% plan backed by a shared default-guarantee pool; (4) conventional credit. One application, one payout to the clinic in 24-48 hours, with compliance reporting for funders.
why_now: The Duffield Foundation committed $250M over 5 years on Sept 17, 2026 (first grants: 250 x $10K plus $10M multi-year), building on PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge. Neither has pipes for high-volume, low-friction placement. Insurance premiums are up 19.7% against animals up 9%, and clinics are being coached on money conversations. Instant payment rails let clinics be paid the same day.
revenue_model: Clinics pay 1-2% of routed funding or $199 a month. Funders pay about 5% of grant flow as an admin fee, which is cheaper than their own staff. Lenders pay origination fees.
non_obvious_insight: The decline decision is made in a 90-second front-desk moment, and every funding source is built for a different moment. Whoever owns the estimate document owns the routing, and philanthropic money is desperate for a distribution pipe with audit trails.
first_30_days: Sign 15 independent clinics in one metro and run the waterfall as a concierge service with spreadsheets and email. Approach one small pet charity and apply as an infrastructure partner to the Duffield programme. Find one claim-advance lender willing to take insurer-receivable risk on a pilot basis.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Downstream Buyers
one_liner: A contingency recovery-audit firm that claws back tariff surcharges buyers paid on duties their suppliers have since had refunded.
customer: CFOs, AP and purchasing teams at $20M-$1B manufacturers and distributors that paid itemized supplier 'tariff surcharges' in 2025-26.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20. By 2026-07-10 CBP had accepted about $121.75B in claims and repaid about $86.3B. Many suppliers billed explicit surcharges (one shop-floor post cites 2.7%) to fund those duties, and they are now collecting refunds on the same money. Buyers assume the refund belongs to the importer of record, and AP treats surcharge lines as noise.
solution: Ingest 18 months of AP data from the ERP or QuickBooks. Use LLM extraction on invoices and price-increase emails to find surcharge lines. Rank suppliers by likely refunded exposure (product HTS and the IEEPA rate window). Generate credit-memo demands and negotiation scripts. Escalate to counsel only for large amounts. Recovery depends on invoice and contract language, and most cases settle as credits against future invoices.
why_now: Refunds are paying out in phases right now, so suppliers hold the cash today. Contract dispute windows are open and evidence is fresh.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency fee on recovered cash or credits. Optional $5k flat fee for a scan of the last 12 months of AP.
non_obvious_insight: The strongest and cheapest claim to a refund often belongs to the downstream buyer holding an itemized surcharge, not the importer. Recovery-audit firms hunt duplicate payments, not tariffs. Buyers also avoid asking for fear of damaging the supplier relationship, so an anonymous third party has an edge.
first_30_days: Sign 5 mid-market manufacturers for a free 12-month surcharge scan. Have counsel draft one template letter. Send the first demands and measure realized recovery. First credit memos should land within 60-90 days.

title: Alternative-Use Memos for Office Special Servicers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, five-day, non-conflicted resolution memo (convert, hold, sell, owner-user sale) for distressed office loans, written for the asset status report.
customer: CMBS special servicers, directing certificateholders (B-piece buyers), CRE CLO managers and bank special-assets groups handling office loans.
problem: About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, $39B matures within 12 months, and 71% of distressed balance is refinance failure rather than missed payments. Advice comes from brokers paid on transactions, and the standard resolution package (appraisal and broker opinion) rarely tests conversion, condo-ization or owner-user sale.
solution: An automated building screen (floor-plate depth, core, window line, structure, zoning, incentives, land-value floor) plus a local architect and contractor sanity check, delivered as a ranked options memo with recovery ranges, formatted for the asset status report. Public CMBS filings are used to prospect.
why_now: The 2026-2028 maturity wall is large and incentives for conversion are spreading. Vision and language models can screen buildings from public records, and servicers need defensible analysis for decisions that are now contested.
revenue_model: $6-12K per asset, sold in prepaid batches; retainers for servicers with 20+ office assets.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the directing certificateholder who bears the loss and can direct disposition, and the cost is typically reimbursable from the loan and trivial against a $50M balance. A conflict-free second opinion can move recovery by points.
first_30_days: Use public CMBS filings to list 200 transferred office loans. Send a free sample memo on one publicly identifiable loan to asset managers at 10 mid-tier servicers and 5 directing holders. Price at $7.5K and target three paid pilots.

title: Cap Ledger for the 350-Home Rule
one_liner: An ownership graph that counts which LLCs a single-family rental owner controls, proves grandfathering and build-to-rent exemption, and becomes the audit trail lenders and buyers demand.
customer: SFR operators and funds with 100-2,000 homes (the almost-institutional tier), their lenders and securitization arrangers, and M&A counsel doing diligence.
problem: The ROAD to Housing Act caps institutional single-family-rental owners at 350 homes, exempts build-to-rent and grandfathers existing owners, but leaves key definitions and reporting mechanics unspecified. Owners hold homes through hundreds of LLCs and JVs, and nobody can currently prove a per-owner count, per-home acquisition date or build-to-rent status.
solution: Build a parcel-level ownership graph from county deeds, mailing addresses, secretary-of-state filings and mortgage records. Output each owner's 'cap position' plus a per-home evidence file (acquisition date, certificate-of-occupancy and first-lease date for BTR). A rules engine updates as regulations finalize, plus a 'what if I buy 60 more homes' scenario tool.
why_now: The cap and grandfathering are new, definitions are ambiguous, and every operator, lender and buyer suddenly needs a defensible number. Whoever's ledger regulators and counterparties adopt sets the standard.
revenue_model: $1-3 per home per year SaaS, $5-15K diligence packages per transaction, and lender portfolio-monitoring licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders read the cap as a threat to institutional SFR, but a cap on new purchases makes grandfathered portfolios scarce capacity and makes provable status a balance-sheet asset. The graph also reveals 'independent' operators that are secretly affiliated, which is valuable to both sides. Sell the ledger, not a fixed reading of rules that will move.
first_30_days: Build the graph for two metros (for example Atlanta and Phoenix) from public deed data. Rank the top 50 owners and cold-email operators in the 100-1,000 home band with their own cap-position PDF. Convert 3 into $10K design-partner pilots. Retain an attorney to track rulemaking.

title: 1098-VLI Reporting for Small Auto Lenders
one_liner: Turn a loan tape into IRS-ready Form 1098-VLI statements, with VIN validation and U.S.-final-assembly flags, for credit unions, community banks and buy-here-pay-here dealers that cannot wait for their core vendor.
customer: Credit unions, community banks, CDFIs, independent auto finance companies, buy-here-pay-here dealers and their loan servicers. Any trade or business receiving $600 or more in interest on a qualifying vehicle loan must report, and the statute has no small-lender exemption. The lender pays per form and per VIN cleanse.
problem: Treasury's final regulations under IRC 6050AA (published Sept 8, 2026; effective Nov 9, 2026) require Form 1098-VLI showing borrower TIN, interest received, opening principal, origination date and the vehicle's year, make, model and VIN. Statements are due to borrowers by Jan 31 and to the IRS by Feb 28 (Mar 31 if e-filed), with penalties under 6721 and 6722. Transition relief covered 2025, so the 2026 tax year is the first full-form season. The preamble concedes lenders 'may need to collect additional information' and 'may experience difficulties accurately reporting the VIN'. Treasury declined to make lenders verify U.S. assembly, allowing reliance on the VIN plant code or the manufacturer's final-assembly label.
solution: The lender uploads a CSV from its core or loan origination system. The service validates VIN check digits, decodes them through NHTSA's free decoder, and maps plant-of-manufacture codes through a curated plant-to-final-assembly table it maintains. It screens for new versus used, personal use and origination date, and checks TIN completeness. It produces an exception queue (missing or wrong VINs) with borrower outreach templates. It then generates and delivers the 1098-VLI statements and e-files with the IRS. A white-label web widget for lender sites answers 'is my loan deduction-eligible?'
why_now: The regs were finalized Sept 8, 2026 and take effect Nov 9. Statements are due Jan 31, 2027, giving four months. Big core processors will serve their largest clients first, and 2026 is the first year without a simple summary-statement safe harbor. The consumer deduction (up to $10,000 of interest on new, U.S.-assembled vehicles under the 2025 tax law) means borrowers will call their lenders asking whether their car qualifies.
revenue_model: $2-4 per form with a $1,500 annual minimum. $0.25 per loan for VIN cleansing and exception handling. Enterprise license for servicers and core-vendor partners. Consumer eligibility widget with lead-gen to tax preparers or refinance offers.
non_obvious_insight: Treasury turned a bright-line rule into a data-quality problem and pushed the risk to the lender. Whether a car is American-assembled is answered by plant-code tables and labels, not by anything in a lender's servicing system, and the preamble openly warns of VIN reporting difficulties. The moat is a curated plant-to-final-assembly table plus an exceptions workflow, which the big vendors will treat as an edge case for small clients. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/08/2026-18219/car-loan-interest-deduction (final regs on 6050AA reporting, Form 1098-VLI, the $600 threshold, no small-lender exemption, and the VIN and plant-of-manufacture provisions).
first_30_days: Build the VIN pipeline on NHTSA's free decoder and validate it on 1,000 real VINs. Offer 30 credit unions a free VIN readiness audit on a 500-loan sample tape and show them their error rate. Publish a plant-code explainer for CU and community bank newsletters. Sign three design partners through state credit union leagues and CUSOs, with a goal of $10k in prepaid annual minimums by December.

title: Tariff Refund Rescue for Micro-Importers
one_liner: A flat-fee triage, protest and pooled-filing service that recovers IEEPA tariff refunds for small importers whose entries fell outside the automated CBP refund system.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $5K-$250K of IEEPA duties paid: direct-import Shopify/Amazon/Etsy sellers, small distributors, restaurants and retailers who imported containers. Not the big players, who already have trade lawyers. They pay a flat audit fee plus a success fee on money recovered. Lenders and claim buyers are a secondary customer.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP's CAPE refund portal opened Apr 20 and initially covered only about 63% of entries. Entries that were finally liquidated, are under protest, or have mixed statuses fall outside it. The 180-day protest clock runs per entry. Trade lawyers quote $10,000-$15,000, which wipes out a $15,000 refund. Small importers hold these stuck entries and cannot justify the fees, while interest accrues at 6%.
solution: Software plus a small ops desk. The importer uploads ACE reports or grants read-only ACE access. The tool sorts every entry into CAPE-eligible, protest window still open (with a per-entry deadline calendar), or finally liquidated. It auto-builds CAPE declarations for self-filers, protest packets, and a standardized pooled Court of International Trade joinder or complaint filed by a partner trade law firm at a flat per-importer price. It also verifies and bundles small claims into $20M+ pools that lenders and claim buyers will finance. That gives importers cash now instead of a 60-90+ day wait. Non-lawyers cannot share legal fees, so the legal work is a separate flat fee to partner counsel.
why_now: CAPE Phase 1 opened Apr 20, 2026 and Phase 2 on Jun 29. The CIT issued reliquidation orders for finally liquidated entries on Jul 15 and Jul 21, but it is unclear whether non-litigants must sue. In late September 2026, coverage says refunds remain 'caught between Customs and the courts'. Protest windows on spring-2026 liquidations are expiring right now. The Feb-Sept 2026 window will not repeat.
revenue_model: $99-$299 triage fee, credited toward a 7-12% success fee on refunds recovered (software and ops, not legal fees). A flat pass-through fee to partner counsel for CIT filings. Portfolio-packaging fee, paid by the lender or claim buyer, on pooled small claims that meet institutional minimums.
non_obvious_insight: The money is in the long tail, not the big importers. The US Chamber says 300,000+ companies and about $166B in duties are affected, across 53M+ entries (https://www.uschamber.com/economy/tariff-refunds-faq-what-small-businesses-need-to-know-after-supreme-courts-ruling). A Sept 2026 report says small importers are stuck because $10K-$15K legal costs can exceed the refund itself, and that importers have entries spread across unliquidated, protest-window and final statuses at the same time (https://kvia.com/stacker-international/2026/09/22/months-after-ieepa-tariffs-were-struck-down-some-refunds-remain-caught-between-customs-and-the-courts/). Meanwhile the refund-claims secondary market is estimated at up to $100B, trading at up to 60 cents on the dollar, but lenders want a minimum $10M loan against at least $20M of claims (https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/04/ieepa-tariff-refund-claims-key-considerations-for-lenders-borrowers-and-claims-purchasers). Nobody aggregates the small claims. The wedge is a per-entry deadline calendar and standardized filing packet, plus pooling for liquidity, not legal advice.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build an ACE-report parser that outputs entry buckets and protest deadlines, and sign a flat-fee arrangement with a licensed customs broker and a CIT-admitted trade attorney. Days 8-20: post the free 'which of my entries are stuck?' triage tool in small-importer communities (Shopify and Amazon private-label groups, freight forwarder mailing lists, Reddit r/importing). Target 30 uploads. Days 21-30: convert 8-10 importers to paid protest or pooled filings, and record the recovered dollars as case studies for the lender pooling pitch.

title: Certified Coder Audit Pods for Autonomous Coding
one_liner: Displaced medical coders, organised as credentialed audit pods, provide the sampled human sign-off that lets hospitals trust autonomous coding AI to submit claims.
customer: Autonomous medical-coding vendors who need a human audit layer to close hospital deals, hospital revenue-cycle compliance leaders and physician groups. Pricing is $1.5-4 per audited chart or $15-40k a month per pod.
problem: Coding is a highly exposed white-collar job, and coders are being cut as autonomous coding reaches production. But billing compliance (False Claims Act exposure, payer and RAC audits) needs accountable, credentialed review. Vendors' own audit teams are thin or offshore and unlicensed.
solution: Pods of 5-10 CPC/CCS-certified ex-coders with a lead auditor, receiving risk-stratified samples of AI-coded charts via API. They provide error-taxonomy dashboards, monthly compliance attestations, feedback loops that retrain the model and contractual accuracy thresholds.
why_now: Autonomous coding moved into production in 2025-26, the coder job pool is shrinking, payers are using AI audits themselves and hospital margins are under pressure.
revenue_model: Per-chart fees or pod retainers at 45-55% gross margin, plus premium attestation packages.
non_obvious_insight: Full automation in healthcare billing stalls at the accountability signature, and the people displaced are the ones who can provide it. The human role shifts from doing to auditing a 5-10% sample, which is recurring compliance spend rather than labor cost. The audit data is also valuable training data for the vendor.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 laid-off certified coders through AAPC and AHIMA forums. Pitch 5 autonomous-coding startups a pilot: audit 1,000 charts at about $2 each with a written accuracy report. Sign one as a design partner.

title: Duty Refund Claims Desk for Small Importers
one_liner: Over $100B in tariff refunds are flowing, but small importers can't afford the paperwork. Run the filing, deadline tracking and refund advance as a service.
customer: Small and mid importers of record ($1M-$50M of annual imports) that paid the struck-down tariffs, plus customs brokers who don't want the grunt work.
problem: Refunds are flowing but small importers face records, liquidation and protest deadlines, multiple brokers and bonds, and filing costs ('not without a cost,' Colorado Sun, 2026-07-02). The government is fighting an order to refund all importers (WaPo, 2026-08-11). Brokers are paid per entry, not per refund, so nobody chases.
solution: Connect customs-entry data from the importer's broker, identify eligible entries and deadlines, file protests and post-summary corrections through a partner licensed customs broker, and track each claim to payment. Offer an advance of about 80% of approved claims at a discount, funded by a small credit facility.
why_now: Refunds have passed $100B (CNBC 2026-08-07, Forbes 2026-09-09) with litigation ongoing. Twenty-five states are challenging the replacement Section 122 tariffs, so a second claim wave may follow.
revenue_model: 10-15% success fee on recovered duties, plus a 2-3% monthly discount on advances once financing is in place.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck isn't law, it's data assembly and deadline hygiene. The refund often lands in a broker's account or gets stuck for lack of a clear owner. Small importers who recover cash are also the source of pass-through claims for the downstream-recovery business.
first_30_days: Sign a licensed customs broker as partner. Recruit 20 importers through marketplace-seller communities and manufacturer associations. Process five entries by hand end to end and collect the first success fees.

title: Special-Tool Exchange for Retiring Regional Fleets
one_liner: Buy or take on consignment the OEM special tooling stranded when regionals retire 50-seat jets and older turboprops, calibrate it, and rent or sell it to operators who cannot get it from the OEM for months.
customer: MROs and Part 145 shops adding a regional-jet or turboprop type, Part 135 and cargo operators, freighter-conversion programs, and operators in Latin America, Africa and Asia flying older regional types. Sellers are regional airlines and lessors with tooling cages to empty.
problem: Every type needs OEM special tooling: rigging pins, wing and gear jack adapters, engine sling adapters, pinning tools, pressure-test rigs, borescope adapters, prop and control-rigging fixtures. New from the OEM this is expensive and lead times can run to months, and some tooling is out of production. When a regional retires a subfleet, that tooling is on the tool-control ledger at near-zero book value, taking up cage space. It gets scrapped, shipped out with airframes, or forgotten. Buyers who are desperate for it have no idea the seller exists, and vice versa.
solution: A consignment marketplace and rental pool. Take tooling in from retiring fleets at no cash outlay, on a 70/30 split of sales and rentals. Inspect it, get it recalibrated through a metrology lab, tag it with a certificate, and catalog it with photos and drawing references. Rent it weekly or monthly with a deposit and freight, or sell it. Offer starter tooling bundles for a shop taking on a new type, such as everything needed for a first C-check on that airframe.
why_now: Majors keep replacing 50-seat regional jets and older turboprops with larger regional aircraft, so tooling cages empty every quarter. Cargo conversions and second-life operators in emerging markets are keeping the old types flying. OEM lead times and parts availability have been poor across the industry since 2022, so buyers will pay to skip the wait.
revenue_model: Consignment split on sales, rental fees at roughly 3-6% of replacement value per month, calibration and freight margin, and bundle pricing for new-type start-ups. Later, a subscription for shops that want guaranteed access to a tooling pool.
non_obvious_insight: Tooling has none of the obsolescence problem of parts. It does not expire except for calibration. A directors of maintenance would rather give it away than pay to store it, and nobody knows who the buyers are. The unusual thing about this business is that the inventory is almost free and the demand is urgent, because a missing pin can ground an airplane for weeks.
first_30_days: Call 20 directors of maintenance, tech-services managers and lessor technical reps whose subfleets are winding down. Get two or three tool cages on consignment with no upfront cash. Photograph and catalog them, send calibrated items to a local metrology lab, and publish a simple catalog with rental terms and a deposit process. Contact freighter-conversion programs, Part 135 operators and international MROs that fly the same type. The first rental should close within weeks, because the urgency price is high.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Desk for Small Platforms
one_liner: Outsourced 48-hour notice-and-removal operations (intake, requester verification, adjudication, audit logs) for forums, hosts and indie social apps.
customer: Small and mid-size platforms with user-generated content (forums, image hosts, creator platforms, community apps, dating apps) that have no trust-and-safety staff, plus web hosts and their counsel.
problem: The FTC began enforcing the TAKE IT DOWN Act on 19 May 2026, wrote to 15 large platforms including Discord, Reddit and Automattic, and lists civil penalties of $53,088 per violation. Coverage reaches forums with user content. The 48-hour clock is real, but the request process is abusable, since false takedown notices can be weaponised, and platforms must verify that the requester is the depicted person without collecting more sensitive imagery.
solution: A hosted intake endpoint and a staffed desk. It offers identity-light requester verification (hash matching in the style of StopNCII), adjudication by trained reviewers with escalation, removal of known identical copies across the customer's site, an appeal and counter-notice path, and FTC-ready audit logs. Follow-the-sun contractors with wellness support provide coverage. Requires legal review per jurisdiction.
why_now: Enforcement started in May 2026, the FTC opened a complaint portal (TakeItDown.ftc.gov), and nonconsensual deepfake volume is rising. Small platforms cannot afford in-house teams, and the statute imposes a duty to act with no penalty for false requests.
revenue_model: $500-5k per month base plus $15-40 per resolved case, with enterprise SLAs.
non_obvious_insight: The statute mandates speed but not accuracy, so the operational risk is over-removal and abuse. The product is adjudication with a paper trail, not filtering, and the buyer's fear is an FTC letter, not a bad user.
first_30_days: Sell through forum-software hosting partners, web-hosting providers and indie creator platforms. Train a contractor pool in handling sensitive imagery and stand up intake for 10 pilot communities.

title: Launch Kits for the First Psilocybin Clinics
one_liner: A readiness and operations service that helps ketamine and TMS clinics and state-licensed psilocybin centers get staffed, compliant and billable before the first FDA approval.
customer: Interventional psychiatry clinics (ketamine, TMS, Spravato sites) and state-licensed psilocybin service centers in Oregon and Colorado, paying $8-20k for a readiness audit plus $3-6k a month for ops software.
problem: Trend chain: Compass's COMP360 has positive phase 3 data and a new CEO (Sep 2026) for a 'coming launch', so an approval is plausible within about a year (timing uncertain). Then treatment needs 6-8 hour monitored dosing sessions with trained monitors, recovery rooms, screening, integration follow-up and prior authorization. Then the sites have four times the chair-time of Spravato, no proven billing model, and some Oregon centers have already closed for lack of economics.
solution: Phase 1: a readiness audit covering space design, staffing model, screening protocol, day-long-session P&L, and payer mix, plus monitor training through partners. Phase 2: ops software for scheduling day-long sessions, pooling monitors across clinics, integration follow-up, REMS-style reporting and prior-auth packets.
why_now: Compass is preparing filing and launch. Oregon's program is live and Colorado opened licensed healing centers in 2025, so a paying pilot audience exists today. The 2024 FDA rejection of Lykos's MDMA showed how much process rigor matters. Ketamine clinics are consolidating and want a new line.
revenue_model: Readiness audit fee, monthly ops subscription, training seat fees, and a margin on a shared monitor staffing pool.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for the first psychedelic drug is chair-hours, not efficacy: 6-8 staffed hours per treatment with no settled reimbursement. The team that builds the day-long-session P&L and staffing model first owns the picks-and-shovels position.
first_30_days: Interview 20 ketamine and TMS clinic owners and 5 Oregon or Colorado center owners. Publish a free 'psilocybin chair-hour P&L calculator' to capture leads. Sell three readiness audits at $8-10k.

title: Agentic Crypto Trace-and-Freeze Desk for Police
one_liner: An AI forensic analyst that traces a victim's stolen crypto across chains in minutes and drafts freeze requests, sold to local police who receive these reports but cannot trace.
customer: Police and sheriff's fraud and elder-crimes units, state AG consumer units, victim-service nonprofits and credit unions.
problem: Crypto-related complaints hit 181,565 and $11.4B in 2025, and victims report to local police who lack $20K+ blockchain forensics tools and training. Funds hop through swaps, bridges and exchange deposit addresses, and freeze windows are measured in hours.
solution: An officer or victim enters a transaction hash and an agent traces flows across major chains and bridges, clusters to exchange deposit addresses using open labels, and produces a freeze packet (evidence PDF and correctly formatted requests to exchange law-enforcement portals and stablecoin issuers). The officer approves, and recovery outcomes are tracked.
why_now: Tool-using agents can now run chain-analysis workflows and draft legal requests. Stablecoin issuers are cooperating on freezes at scale, and scam flows concentrate in a few tokens and exchanges.
revenue_model: $3-10K per agency per year, or about $150 per case, with elder-justice grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in crypto recovery is procedural delivery, not analytics: which desk accepts what format, and how fast. An agent that sends the right request in minutes matters more than another dashboard.
first_30_days: Build tracing for USDT on Tron and Ethereum plus Bitcoin to the top 10 exchanges. Offer free traces to 10 sheriff's offices, track freezes, publish outcomes, and start $250 per month pilots with elder-justice grant funding lined up.

title: Tenant Childcare Consortium Powered by 45F Credits
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate (office/medical office landlords, vacancy) x Employer childcare
one_liner: Turn a vacant floor in a multi-tenant office or medical office building into a shared licensed childcare center whose seats are bought by 10-40 small tenant employers, each claiming the expanded 45F credit through a landlord-led consortium.
customer: Landlords of class-B office and medical office buildings (setup and management fee), small employers in those buildings (compliance fee and seat purchases), and a specialist childcare operator.
problem: Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally and lenders face $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months, so landlords need sticky tenants. Small employers cannot justify their own center. From 2026 the 45F credit is 40% (50% for small businesses) of qualified childcare spending, capped at $500K ($600K), and the law now lets an intermediary contract with childcare facilities for several employers. Almost no one has built the intermediary. Hospitals, clinics and professional-services firms in medical office buildings have severe shift-worker childcare gaps.
solution: The landlord donates or discounts a vacant suite (ideally lower floors) and a TI allowance. A licensed operator runs the center. The platform acts as the intermediary entity: it signs seat contracts with 10-40 tenants, documents each employer's qualified expenditure for the credit (Form 8882), pools and re-allocates unused seats among tenants, and helps employees route the DCFSA. A third-party operator whose principal business is childcare also sidesteps the 30%-employee-enrollment test that trips up in-house employer centers (to be confirmed with tax counsel).
why_now: The OBBBA expansion took effect for tax years beginning after Dec 31, 2025, so employers are setting 2026 and 2027 budgets now, and the year-end rush to lock 2026 credits is a natural sales moment. Landlords are under maturity-wall pressure and compete on amenities.
revenue_model: Landlord setup fee plus an NOI share of the operating margin (about 10%), a per-employer compliance fee (3-5% of credit value), and operator management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The credit turns a landlord amenity into a purchasing cooperative: alone a 40-person tenant cannot justify a center, but 20 together can, and the credit is richest for exactly the small businesses that fill class-B buildings. A child's seat is also far stickier than free rent as a lease-renewal driver, because losing the lease means losing the seat.
first_30_days: Approach five owners of medical office buildings and suburban office parks with 20%+ vacancy in a high-cost childcare metro. Survey tenants with a two-question form to size seat demand. Line up an operator and a tax counsel opinion memo. Aim to sign 8-10 employer seat contracts before December 2026 so they capture credits for this tax year.

title: Cell-Type-Restricted Promoters for Safer AAV
one_liner: AI-designed, primary-cell-validated regulatory sequences that switch AAV or LNP transgenes on only in target tissues and off in the liver.
customer: Gene therapy developers in muscle, heart and CNS (DMD, LGMD, cardiomyopathies) and capsid or CDMO companies wanting a detargeting cassette.
problem: High-dose systemic AAV caused acute liver failure deaths in 2025: three Sarepta patients, followed by a boxed warning and removal of non-ambulatory eligibility by Nov 14, 2025. Capsid engineering gets the attention, but the expression cassette is a second lever. Common promoters (CMV, CAG) are strong but non-specific, and miR-122 target sites only partly suppress liver expression.
solution: Generative design plus MPRA in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle cells and in primary human hepatocytes, ranking 10^4-10^5 sequences for high target and low liver expression. Deliver compact promoter-enhancer sets (under ~500 bp) with an optional miR-detargeting cassette, validated in vitro and in one partner rodent or NHP pilot.
why_now: The 2025 safety crisis is pushing dose reduction and liver detargeting. MPRA and generative sequence models are mature, DNA is cheap, and FDA's move toward human-relevant methods favors human primary-cell data.
revenue_model: $150-300k design-and-validation project plus a $50-200k license, with milestones or light royalties.
non_obvious_insight: The industry over-indexes on capsids, yet toxicity tracks where the transgene is expressed at dose. Compact regulatory parts are modular IP that stacks with any capsid, so one library serves many developers.
first_30_days: Run an MPRA on about 20k designed sequences in iPSC cardiomyocytes versus hepatocytes ($40-60k in reagents and sequencing). Publish a preprint and pitch 15 DMD, LGMD and cardiac programs on $50k pilots.

title: Slop-Rating Feed for Kids' Filters
one_liner: A channel- and app-level data feed that classifies children's content as verified human-made, AI slop or unknown, sold to school web filters and kids' hardware.
customer: School-district web-filter and parental-control vendors, kids' tablet, audio-player and smart-speaker makers, and school districts directly.
problem: Fairplay found that 104 of the first 500 videos recommended to a fresh account were AI slop. On 1 Apr 2026 more than 200 organisations, including the American Federation of Teachers, asked YouTube to label and ban AI content on kids' surfaces, and YouTube said only that it is developing labels. Filters classify by topic (violence, adult), not by how content was produced.
solution: Continuously crawl kids-targeted channels, apps, audiobooks and games. Classify provenance using channel behaviour, voice and image-model signals, upload cadence and template reuse, plus human review. Add a 'verified human-made' tier through creator attestations and audits. Deliver category lists by API keyed on channel ID, domain or app package, plus teacher whitelist packs.
why_now: Spring 2026 investigations (NYT, Fairplay, CBC) and the April coalition letter made AI slop a school and parent issue. The EU AI Act's Article 50 labelling is beginning, and 1:1 school device fleets need a new filter category now.
revenue_model: $20-200k per year data licences to filter vendors, $0.10-0.50 per-device royalties from hardware makers, and $1-3 per student per year for districts.
non_obvious_insight: A platform's own AI label will always be optional and gameable. The buyer is whoever sits between the child and the platform, and they already buy category feeds. Selling a new dimension (provenance) into an existing distribution channel avoids consumer acquisition entirely.
first_30_days: Build a 20k-channel labelled seed set with three teacher or parent reviewers. Ship a free 'slop score' browser extension for teachers to collect signals and leads. Pitch three mid-size filter and parental-control vendors with a sample feed.

title: Closing-Risk Radar for New-Construction Loan Officers
one_liner: Forecasts which locked new-build closings will miss their rate-lock window, using permit and inspection data plus builder history, so loan officers extend cheaply or re-price before the buyer walks.
customer: New-construction loan officers and mortgage teams (builder-preferred lenders, community banks), title companies, and small builders' sales managers.
problem: 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns, and completions fell 27.1% as crews vanish, foundations sit idle and electricians are delayed up to 2 months. Closing dates slip, locks expire and buydown funding is stranded. A West Virginia builder is at risk of losing about 40 closings. Nobody forecasts construction slippage, only rates.
solution: For each locked loan, ingest the address and pull permit and inspection status from municipal portals, add the builder's stage photos or one-question SMS replies, and output a slip probability and the cheapest date to extend. Add a monthly builder reliability scorecard for lender risk and builder-relations teams.
why_now: Buydown-dependent sales, mortgage rates near 7%, falling completions and forecast 2027 starts down 2-4% mean lock-expiry losses will climb. LLM-based extraction from messy municipal portals is now cheap.
revenue_model: $25-50 per monitored loan or $400-800 per month per loan officer. Enterprise scorecards for lender risk teams.
non_obvious_insight: Loan officers care about the construction calendar as much as the rate curve, and they have direct fee income at stake when a lock lapses, unlike builders who learn late. Public inspection sequence is a surprisingly strong predictor of slip, and the reliability scorecard is a byproduct with its own buyer.
first_30_days: Sell to five new-construction loan officers in Texas and the Southeast. Each shares 20-40 pending closings. Build the forecast manually in spreadsheets from portals and show five saves in 30 days.

title: Child-in-the-Room Detector for Voice AI
one_liner: A tiny on-device SDK that infers from a few seconds of speech whether a speaker is likely a child, so voice assistants, cars, TVs and toys can drop into a safe policy tier without any login, camera or ID.
customer: OEMs of smart speakers, TVs and in-car assistants, voice-AI and companion app makers, and toy makers.
problem: Ambient voice AI serves shared households with no account or age signal. Laws and probes (CA SB 243, the FTC 6(b) inquiry, COPPA 'actual knowledge') create duties once a minor is present. Devices cannot tell a child from an adult, and asking kids to log in fails. The amended COPPA rule's biometric coverage makes storing voiceprints risky.
solution: An SDK under 5MB that classifies speaker age band (under 9, 9-15, adult) with calibrated confidence and an abstain option, using ephemeral features and never storing voiceprints. It returns a 'minor-likely' signal to trigger safe modes (topic limits, no romance roleplay, safe-messaging protocols) with audit logs. It is benchmarked publicly across accents and speech differences and fails safe by default.
why_now: Lawsuits and the FTC inquiry are pushing platforms to prove they detect minors, on-device speech encoders are good enough, and the brief flags a demand for privacy-preserving, non-ID age signals.
revenue_model: Per-device royalty of $0.10-0.50 or per-MAU pricing, plus paid integration and benchmark-certification services.
non_obvious_insight: For a voice product, the best age signal is the voice itself, with no ID, camera or login. The error costs are asymmetric: treating an adult as a child is cheap, the reverse is not, so 'fail safe' is the sales pitch.
first_30_days: Fine-tune an open speech encoder on licensed or consented child and adult speech corpora. Publish an open benchmark and baseline. Talk to 10 voice-AI and toy builders. Land 2 paid pilots at $3-5k each.

title: CRA Technical-File Compiler Built Into CI
one_liner: A GitHub/GitLab app that assembles the Cyber Resilience Act technical documentation, Annex I evidence and draft declaration of conformity from every release, so compliance is a build artifact rather than a consulting project.
customer: Product-security leads and CTOs at connected-device makers with 20-300 engineers (smart home, industrial IoT, e-bikes, wearables, network gear, EV chargers) selling into the EU. Not the GRC team.
problem: CRA reporting duties began 11 Sep 2026, full application is 11 Dec 2027, and fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Manufacturers must keep versioned technical documentation (risk assessment, design, vulnerability handling, test evidence, SBOM), for roughly ten years or the support period. GRC platforms produce policy evidence, SBOM tools produce component lists, and consultants charge tens of thousands per product line for a file that goes stale on the next release.
solution: The app reads the repo, CI logs, SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX), threat-model files and test results, then maps them to the Annex I essential requirements and vulnerability-handling duties. It posts gaps as pull-request comments ('no secure-update mechanism documented'). Each release yields a signed, timestamped technical-file bundle (PDF plus machine-readable), a declaration-of-conformity draft, a support-period statement and a diff from the previous release.
why_now: Reporting is already live and full application is 15 months away, so products in design today are locking in the choices that determine compliance cost. Harmonised standards are still arriving, so teams need structured evidence now rather than a finished standard to tick off.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1,500-6,000/month per product line, EUR 5-15k onboarding, and referral revenue from test labs and notified bodies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume Vanta/Drata-style GRC platforms will absorb the CRA. But the CRA is product regulation: the evidence lives in Git, CI and design docs and must be regenerated each release. That is a developer-tool, bottom-up sale to engineers, not a compliance-officer sale.
first_30_days: Interview 15 device makers via CRA meetups and open-source foundations working on CRA. Build a CLI that ingests a CycloneDX SBOM plus a small cra.yaml and emits a skeleton technical file. Run three paid pilots (EUR 3-5k) that produce each firm's first file, and publish the Annex I checklist as open source to draw inbound.

title: Scam-Baiting AI Fleet Selling Mule Intel
one_liner: Thousands of realistic AI victims answer scammers' calls and chats around the clock, extract the accounts and wallets they are told to pay, and hand them to the holding institutions before real victims do.
customer: Banks, neobanks, BaaS sponsor banks, stablecoin issuers, exchanges and payment apps. Telcos are a secondary buyer.
problem: Scam cash-out depends on mule accounts and wallets, but institutions learn about them only after victims pay. Scam revenue reached about $17B in 2025, and AI-enabled operations earn far more per operation, while defense stays manual and reactive.
solution: Persona-driven voice and messaging agents on real-time speech-to-speech models answer phone numbers seeded onto scam lead lists and respond to smishing and wrong-number openers. They keep scammers engaged (burning their labor), record payment instructions, and extract payee accounts, wallets and gift-card destinations. Evidence-graded indicators go via API to the institution that holds the account so it can freeze and close before a real victim pays.
why_now: Real-time speech models made convincing multi-turn calls cheap in 2025-26. Stablecoin issuers and cross-industry units now freeze funds quickly, and the US-UK scam-center coordination raises appetite for actionable intelligence.
revenue_model: $200-1,000 per confirmed account or wallet plus $5-20K per month subscriptions, and data licensing to fraud vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Scammers' scarce resource is human operator time, so AI victims raise their cost per victim while producing intelligence with zero victim cost. Institutions pay far more for pre-loss intelligence than for post-loss forensics.
first_30_days: Build 20 personas across phone and WhatsApp. Run them against inbound spam numbers and produce about 100 verified indicators. Sell 2 neobanks and 1 exchange a $10K paid pilot, with counsel reviewing recording-consent rules first.

title: Crash-Test Ratings for Collusive Pricing Agents
one_liner: A simulation lab and clean-room negotiation venue that certifies your pricing or negotiating agent does not tacitly collude with counterpart agents, like Euro NCAP for antitrust.
customer: General counsel, antitrust counsel and pricing or procurement heads at companies deploying pricing or negotiation agents: property managers and landlords, hotels, insurers, freight brokers, ad-buying agencies and retailers. Pricing-software vendors who are being sued are the first buyers.
problem: Two LLM agents that repeatedly interact can converge on supracompetitive prices with no human ever agreeing to anything. The law is moving fast: California's AB 325 took effect January 1, 2026, the DOJ RealPage settlement landed in late 2025, and DOJ officials said in May 2026 that 'software cannot launder collusion'. Deployers have no way to show their agent is clean.
solution: A harness that plays your agent against a zoo of counterpart agents (clones of itself, competitor-like agents, vendor agents) across thousands of repeated-game scenarios. It measures price convergence, punishment and signaling patterns, and information leakage, and issues a rated report plus CI regression tests. A hosted clean-room negotiation venue firewalls competitors' inputs and keeps regulator-readable logs. Partner economists and an antitrust firm sign the report.
why_now: AB 325 and its lowered pleading standard, active DOJ and state enforcement, private class actions over pricing algorithms, and agent-to-agent negotiation going live with the 2026 commerce protocols. Academic work has shown LLM pricing agents can settle on collusive outcomes without instruction.
revenue_model: $25-150k per audit, $2-5k per month for CI-integrated monitoring, and expert-witness and defense-support add-ons revenue-shared with partner economists.
non_obvious_insight: The exculpatory evidence is counterfactual behavior: what your agent would do if a rival raised its price. Only the deployer can generate that evidence, and it is cheap to produce in simulation, so antitrust compliance can be turned into unit tests. Because plausible-agreement pleading is now enough to survive dismissal, having a dated, third-party test record is worth far more than its price.
first_30_days: Team up an industrial-organization economist and an antitrust lawyer. Publish an open 'collusion eval' benchmark of LLM repeated pricing games to build credibility. Pitch 10 rental-pricing, hospitality and freight-pricing software vendors a $25k fixed-fee 'pre-litigation' audit and close the first two within about 60 days.
